greeting: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gathers us today in his love.
penitential:
Lord Jesus, you are the healer of our hearts: Lord, have mercy.
Christ Jesus, you are the companion of our journey: Christ, have mercy.
Lord Jesus, you are the promise of our eternal home: Lord, have mercy.
psalm_response: How great are the works of the Lord!
homily:
In the heart of the home, there is often a small, quiet space where the most important things are kept. Perhaps it is a shelf with a favorite book, or a desk where a project remains unfinished, or simply a spot by the window where the light hits just right in the morning. We all have these anchors of memory—physical, tangible reminders of the people we love. Today, in the Gospel, Jesus enters the home of a Pharisee. It is a setting of tension, of careful observation, but Jesus does not look at the social rules or the expectations of the room. He looks at a man suffering. He sees the person, not the circumstance. He sees the need, not the social protocol. 

I want you to hold onto this image: the gaze of Jesus. It is a gaze that disrupts our rigid structures and replaces them with a radical, life-giving mercy. It is the gaze that looks past the 'should' and the 'ought' to find the 'beloved.'

Let us be honest about the ache. Alan, Thao, Ryan, and all of you who carry the memory of Benjamin Vo in your hearts: it has been four months since he went to be with the Lord. We know that the silence in your home is not a peaceful silence; it is a heavy, ringing absence. You wake up, and for a split second, the world feels normal, and then the reality rushes back in. You look at the places where he used to be—the desk where he coded his games, the spots where he dreamed of 'con chim airlines,' the quiet corners that still hold the echo of his laughter—and the weight of missing him can feel like a mountain. It is an ache that does not ask for platitudes. It is an ache that asks for the truth. And the truth is that you are grieving a loss that is as deep as the love you had for him. You are allowed to be tired. You are allowed to be sad. You are allowed to be human.

There is a temptation, when we carry such a weight, to look back at the path we walked and wonder if we missed a sign. We wonder if we could have seen something earlier, or done something differently, or if we failed in some hidden way. Let us lift that stone from your hearts right now. You missed nothing. You were the parents and the brother that Benjamin was given. You loved him with a completeness that filled his fifteen years with the richness of the world. You walked the globe with him, you shared the meals, you witnessed the brilliance of his mind and the gentleness of his spirit. God does not accuse you, and you must not accuse yourselves. The sorrow that has entered your life is not a consequence of anything you did or failed to do. You were faithful. You were present. You were love in action. Let that burden fall away, and let yourself breathe.

Now, let the Gospel break in. Jesus looks at the man with dropsy. He sees the suffering, and he asks a question that stops the room cold: 'Is it lawful to cure on the sabbath or not?' He is not asking about legalities. He is asking about the heart of God. He is saying that the Sabbath—the day of rest, the day of God—is made for mercy. It is made for healing. It is made for bringing life. Jesus reaches out, he heals the man, and he dismisses him. He restores him to his life, to his family, to his purpose. And then he says something that strikes at the very core of our human connection: 'Who among you, if your son or ox falls into a cistern, would not immediately pull him out on the sabbath day?'

Think of the image of the cistern. It is a place of darkness, of being trapped, of being unable to climb out on one's own. But Jesus says that the love of a father, the love of a family, is stronger than any rule or any obstacle. He is telling you that he is the one who pulls us out. He is the one who reaches into the darkness to bring us into the light. When you feel trapped by your grief, when you feel like you are at the bottom of a cold, dark place, know that Jesus is reaching down. He is not standing back, waiting for you to be 'better' or to 'move on.' He is in the cistern with you. He is the one who lifts you up.

Benjamin was a boy who understood the beauty of connection. Think of his brilliant mind—the way he looked at the world through the lens of mathematics and logic, yet always with a heart that was soft and kind. He was a boy who, at fifteen, offered his entire piggy bank to help an uncle who was struggling. He didn't need to break the bank, he didn't need to empty it—the offer itself was the revelation of his character. It was the movement of a soul that was already living in the Kingdom of God. That is the boy you raised. That is the boy who is now at the banquet of heaven, looking down at you. And just as he was a source of light and joy for you, he continues to be a source of grace. Think of the well in Cà Mau, the clean water flowing for the poor in his name. His love did not end when his life on earth did. It is still flowing. It is still quenching the thirst of the world. It is still doing the work of the Sabbath—the work of mercy, the work of healing.

Ryan, you are a brother who carries a unique, holy weight. You know the memories better than anyone. You know the games you coded, the dreams you shared, the simple, everyday life of being brothers. You are not just a brother who remains; you are a brother who continues the story. When you look at the sky, when you think of the future, remember that you are not doing it alone. You are carrying the legacy of his joy. You are a witness to the world that love is not a finite resource. It is a well that never runs dry. Keep being the boy who reaches out. Keep being the one who values the small, human moments. You are a vital part of this family of four, and your life is a testament to the fact that love is the most durable thing we possess.

We hear in the letter to the Philippians today: 'I am confident of this, that the one who began a good work in you will continue to complete it until the day of Christ Jesus.' This is the promise for Benjamin, and it is the promise for you. The work that God began in Benjamin—the brilliance, the kindness, the curiosity, the love—is not finished. It is being completed in the light of heaven. And the work that God began in you—the love that you gave him, the family you built, the grief you are now carrying—is also being completed. God is not wasting any of your tears. He is gathering them. He is weaving them into the tapestry of his grace.

There is a peace that comes from knowing that we are held. It is not a peace that takes away the pain, but it is a peace that keeps us from being destroyed by it. It is the peace of knowing that Benjamin is waiting. He is waiting in the light, he is waiting in the place where there is no more struggling, no more darkness, only the clear, bright presence of the Father. He is waiting for you with that same sweet, gentle smile that you remember so vividly. That smile is the sign that the work is going well. That smile is the promise that the reunion is certain.

So, what do you carry out the door today? Not a summary, not a heavy burden, but one small, doable thing: when the grief rises and the house feels too quiet, pause. Close your eyes. Imagine the Lord reaching into the cistern, and imagine Benjamin smiling at you from the other side. Let yourself be pulled up. Let yourself be held. And walk out into the world with the quiet, unshakeable hope that the love you share is the most powerful force in the universe. It is stronger than death. It is more enduring than time. And it is the very thing that will bring you home to each other. You are not a broken family. You are a family of four, and you are being held in the palm of God's hand. Keep your heart open to that truth. Keep your eyes on the light. And remember that he is watching over you, always, with love that knows no end. Amen.
petitions: For Benjamin Vo, that he may rest in the light of Christ and enjoy the eternal banquet of heaven, we pray to the Lord.
For all who grieve, that God may console them with his presence and fill their hearts with the hope of the resurrection, we pray to the Lord.
spiritual_communion: My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love You above all things, and I desire to receive You into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace You as if You were already there and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You. Amen.
closing: May the Lord bless you, keep you in his peace, and bring you comfort in your sorrow. Go in the hope of Christ.

readings.label: Reading 1
readings.text:
Paul and Timothy, slaves of Christ Jesus,
to all the holy ones in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi,
with the bishops and deacons:
grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you,
praying always with joy in my every prayer for all of you,
because of your partnership for the Gospel
from the first day until now.
I am confident of this,
that the one who began a good work in you
will continue to complete it
until the day of Christ Jesus.
It is right that I should think this way about all of you,
because I hold you in my heart,
you who are all partners with me in grace,
both in my imprisonment
and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel.
For God is my witness,
how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus.
And this is my prayer:
that your love may increase ever more and more
in knowledge and every kind of perception,
to discern what is of value,
so that you may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ,
filled with the fruit of righteousness
that comes through Jesus Christ
for the glory and praise of God.

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
R. (2) How great are the works of the Lord!
or:
R. Alleluia.
I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart
in the company and assembly of the just.
Great are the works of the LORD,
exquisite in all their delights.
R. How great are the works of the Lord!
or:
R. Alleluia.
Majesty and glory are his work,
and his justice endures forever.
He has won renown for his wondrous deeds;
gracious and merciful is the LORD.
R. How great are the works of the Lord!
or:
R. Alleluia.
He has given food to those who fear him;
he will forever be mindful of his covenant.
He has made known to his people the power of his works,
giving them the inheritance of the nations.
R. How great are the works of the Lord!
or:
R. Alleluia.

readings.label: Gospel
readings.text:
On a sabbath Jesus went to dine
at the home of one of the leading Pharisees,
and the people there were observing him carefully.
In front of him there was a man suffering from dropsy.
Jesus spoke to the scholars of the law and Pharisees in reply, asking,
“Is it lawful to cure on the sabbath or not?”
But they kept silent; so he took the man and,
after he had healed him, dismissed him.
Then he said to them   
“Who among you, if your son or ox falls into a cistern,
would not immediately pull him out on the sabbath day?”  
But they were unable to answer his question.

pet_prayers.text: Hey Ben - Been dreaming about you a lot. Hope you're having fun up in heaven. Please look after our family. Remember to come say hi daily. We miss you so much!

Xin Chúa thương nhậm lời Ben, cho Ben được hưởng ngàn thu bình an bên Chúa. Nếu có thể, xin Ben lại ghé thăm anh trong những giấc mơ tiếp theo nhé, dù chỉ là một lời chào hay một nụ cười thân thương như ngày nào.

pet_prayers.text: Ben, my sweet boy, I miss you so much. Thank you for visiting me and Chú Chris last night. He told me he saw you flying a helicopter—so free, joyful, and strong up there. Down here, Mom and I are crying more and more each day. A piece of my heart feels completely dead without you, Ben. Please watch over us, pray for your mom, your brother Ryan, and me, and give us the strength to keep going. We love you forever
